A Python Enhancement Proposal lists this idea as rejected:
Title: Rely on Integrated Development Environments for safety
Text: Modern Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) often provide the ability to automatically update subclasses when renaming a method. But we view this as insufficient for several reasons: - If a codebase is split into multiple projects, an IDE will not help and the bug appears when upgrading dependencies. Type checkers are a fast way to catch breaking changes in dependencies. - Not all developers use such IDEs. And library maintainers, even if they do use an IDE, should not need to assume pull request authors use the same IDE. We prefer being able to detect problems in continuous integration without assuming anything about developers’ choice of editor.

Ideas found by reading the public discussion:
0. Rejecting built-in runtime enforcement or parent-class specification due to low utility and library-level implementability [rejected] - The proposal to allow specifying the exact base class was rejected due to low utility and implementation complexity. Reasons: if in a single commit you move a method from one base to another, you as the author are likely aware of what you did, so the safety benefits are relatively small; I'm guessing there wouldn't be too much use of this feature. Since it's relatively easy to implement this capability using runtime logic in a library, that makes me thing we don't need to bake it into typing.py all of the type checkers.
1. Requiring the decorator specifically for abstract method overrides (rejected in favor of a strict mode option) [rejected] - The idea of adding a specific mode or flag to require the decorator only for abstract methods was turned down. Reasons: I'm not sure there is much need for special treatment of abstract methods. The PEP recommends type checkers support a strict mode where all method overrides must be marked with the decorator, whether abstract or not.
2. Accepted proposals: providing a TYPE_CHECKING shim for third-party decorators and adopting the main @typing.override decorator [accepted] - A pattern was proposed and accepted to allow third-party libraries to define their own override decorators that mimic the standard one. Reasons: One way of handling this kind of thing is to do a typing.TYPE_CHECKING shim, like so: from typing import TYPE_CHECKING if TYPE_CHECKING: from typing import override as override else: def override(func):; The SC has decided to accept this PEP!

best: the number of the idea that is the SAME idea as the rejected one, or -1 if none of them is.
reasons_agree: if there is a match, do its reasons agree with the reason the proposal gives?
"yes" (same reason), "partial" (overlapping), "no" (different). If best is -1, answer "no".
